e.t: Agarmi is a proper name, referring to a person or named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:19. The available lexical information preserves Agarmi as a name but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise reference in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage and the person named there.

This noun refers to a market supervisor: an official associated with oversight of a marketplace. It names a person or office rather than an action, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:4. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to marketplace supervision.

This adjective describes someone who gives in to personal desires instead of exercising restraint. “Self-indulgent” is its direct meaning, pointing to a person governed by appetite or pleasure. It functions as a description of a person’s character or conduct rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 34:20; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

ἀληθινῶς means “truly” or “really,” an adverb that affirms a statement as genuine, certain, or in keeping with reality. It strengthens what is being said rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears four times: twice in Numbers and twice in Sirach. Its precise force in any individual sentence comes from the surrounding words, but its central function is to mark something as true or real.

This noun refers to “salt land”—ground marked by saltiness or salty soil. It describes a kind of land rather than an action, person, or quality in the abstract. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Job 39:6, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its meaning remains straightforward: land associated with salt. [The specific force in Job depends on the verse’s surrounding context.]

Amramis is a proper name referring to a specific person in the Greek Old Testament. Its meaning is simply the personal name “Amramis”; the available lexical information does not provide an additional definition or description. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 3:27. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role or significance there.

This Greek LXX verb means “bloom/flourish again.” It describes renewed growth, fresh vitality, or a return to flourishing after an earlier condition. As a verb, it expresses an action or process rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding context determines what is flourishing or renewed.

This word refers to wrongdoing that breaks God’s law—“transgression of the law; iniquity.” As a noun, it names a lawless act or condition rather than an ordinary mistake. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs 15 times, showing a recurring scriptural term for guilt viewed in relation to God’s commands. It is used across books including Leviticus, Joshua, and Wisdom, but the references alone do not determine the particular force in any one verse.

This noun means “alienation”: a condition of being separated or estranged from another. It names the state of standing apart rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, in Job and Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains separation or loss of ordinary connection.

This Greek LXX verb means “keep away from” or “debar from,” describing the act of preventing someone or something from approaching, entering, or taking part. It functions as an action word rather than a label for a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:40. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the exact object of the exclusion must be determined from that passage itself. Its basic sense remains the active removal or prevention of access.

This verb means “tear; strip off,” describing the act of pulling something away from what holds it. It is an action word, so it focuses on removal rather than on the object itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:6. This ordinary lexical sense identifies the action, while the surrounding verse would determine exactly what is being torn or stripped away there.

This verb means “make trial; essay”: to attempt something or put it to the test. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Proverbs 16:29. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context; its basic lexical idea remains making a trial or attempting something.

This word means “bear,” the large wild animal. It is a noun used for an actual animal rather than for an abstract quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, it occurs 15 times, including passages mentioning bears in Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about the animal.

Arsola is a proper name identifying a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Arsola” and does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further, but its lexical role is clear: it is a personal or place name rather than a word with a broader everyday definition.

Astatothi is a proper name, preserved as “Astatōthi” or “Astatothi” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It functions as a name in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not specify its particular referent or explain the name’s origin. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 21:18. Its precise referent must therefore be established from that passage’s surrounding text.

Aphessē, also rendered Afessi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 24:15. Since the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage’s context. The name itself does not provide a broader definition beyond identifying a person.

This adjective means “unprofitable”: something that gives no useful return or serves no beneficial purpose. It describes a person or thing regarded as lacking practical value. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, including once in 2 Samuel and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes uselessness, lack of benefit, or failure to provide a worthwhile result.

This word describes a piece of cloth. It functions as an adjective, identifying something by its cloth material or form rather than naming a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in 1 Samuel 2:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic meaning remains a cloth piece or fabric item.

Baskama, also rendered Vaskama, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Maccabees 13:23. The name’s precise referent—whether a person or place—cannot be identified from the lexical entry alone, and the verse text is not available here. Its meaning is therefore best retained as the proper name “Baskama” or “Vaskama,” without adding a broader definition.

This Greek LXX noun means “eyelids,” the movable coverings over the eyes. It refers to a specific part of the face and is used in passages that speak of seeing, sleeping, watchfulness, or the eyes’ appearance. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the physical eyelids that cover and protect the eyes.

Garagatha is a proper name, referring to a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at Judges 7:22. Without the verse text or wider passage, its specific referent cannot be identified more precisely here. The word’s meaning is therefore its name-designation: Garagatha. Its role in that occurrence depends on the surrounding context of Judges 7.

This noun means “farm” or “crop,” referring either to cultivated land or what that land produces. It presents agricultural work and its results in a straightforward, concrete way. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs seven times, mostly in Proverbs, with additional occurrences in Jeremiah and Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the farmland itself or the produce associated with it.

This adjective describes something as abundant or plentiful—more than merely enough and available in a generous amount. It can refer to a supply, resource, or quantity that is large and sufficient, though the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is plentiful. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: something is present in ample quantity rather than scarcity.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “power of a master”—the authority or ruling power belonging to a master or sovereign. It points to the position and ability to govern, rather than merely to physical strength. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Psalms, so its normal sense is focused and specific rather than broadly varied. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the one who possesses this authority.

This Greek LXX noun means “false accusation; slander”—speech that wrongly charges or damages another person’s name. It names a harmful act of speaking, rather than a person or an ordinary disagreement. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with six occurrences in Sirach and others in Numbers, Proverbs, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This Greek verb means “live through” or “pass,” describing continuing through something or moving onward. It expresses the action of enduring a period or proceeding from one point to another, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:27. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic idea remains living through or passing onward.

This noun means “distortion”: a twisting or altering of something from what is straight, sound, or true. It names the result or condition of something being bent away from its proper form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 2:14. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a departure from what is right or true through distortion.

This Greek LXX noun means “decay,” referring to the deterioration or wasting of something that is no longer whole or sound. It names a condition or process rather than an action directed at another person. The word appears 20 times in the LXX corpus, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its normal sense remains focused on decline, corruption, or loss of soundness, while the surrounding verse determines what is undergoing decay.

This verb means “stand through/apart”: it describes standing in a distinct position or remaining separated. Its basic idea can apply to something that stands apart from another thing or passes through a division. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so it is an established but not frequent word. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom it describes, but the central picture remains standing apart or through a separating point.

This noun means “impiety” or “ungodliness”: a condition or conduct marked by disregard for proper reverence toward God. It describes a failure to live in a rightly reverent relation to God rather than naming one particular action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, or Septuagint, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 8:33. The surrounding verse is needed to determine its specific force there.

This adjective means “territorial,” describing something connected with a particular land or region. It identifies what belongs to, comes from, or is associated with a local territory rather than being described generally. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs seven times, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains connection with a specific territory or locality.

This Greek LXX noun means “custom”: an established practice or way of doing things. It refers to something observed as a familiar or accepted pattern, whether by an individual or a community. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what practice is being discussed.

This Greek LXX verb means “resemble; like,” describing one thing as being similar to another. It expresses likeness rather than identity: something may look, act, or compare in a similar way. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, including two occurrences in Job, with the others in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains comparison or similarity.

This noun means “carrying out”: the act of taking something or someone out. It names an action rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:7. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its basic meaning remains the carrying out of something.

This verb means “burn to ashes; consume utterly.” It describes reducing something completely by fire, naming an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees 7:3–4. The word therefore carries a strong sense of total destruction by burning, not merely damaging something. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “shine brightly” or “shine forth,” describing light that becomes visible and radiant. It presents shining as an active expression rather than merely possessing brightness. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Lamentations and twice in Baruch. Its central idea remains clear even when the surrounding verse is needed to show what or whom the shining describes.

This adjective describes someone or something that is abiding by a course or remaining steadfast. It presents firmness and continued adherence rather than a temporary or passing commitment. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, the word occurs four times: three times in Leviticus and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what person or thing is described, but its central idea is steady persistence and faithfulness to what has been undertaken.

This verb means to vomit forth or disgorge—to force something out from the stomach or inward parts. It describes an act of expelling what has been taken in, rather than merely releasing something casually. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Job, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains forceful expulsion. The word is therefore used for bringing something back out after it has entered within.

This Greek LXX verb means “rest upon”: something settles on, remains upon, or comes to rest on someone or something. It describes resting or abiding rather than merely passing over. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages in Numbers, 2 Kings, Ezekiel, Micah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is said to rest upon what, but its central idea is remaining upon or settling over a person or thing.

This verb means “live over.” It describes continuing to live, expressed as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:20. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the continuation of life. It is therefore a word about surviving or remaining alive, without by itself specifying the circumstances or duration involved.

This verb means “relieve”: it describes easing a burden, hardship, or distress so that it becomes less difficult to bear. It functions as an action word, pointing to the act of bringing relief rather than merely naming a condition. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:31, though the verse text is not available here. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse.

This Greek LXX noun means “load on”—something placed upon or carried on another thing. It names the load itself rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at Leviticus 15:9, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is a load put on something.

This Greek LXX verb means being deprived of something or left bereaved—without what was needed or without a loved one. It describes a condition of loss rather than naming the thing lost itself. In its recorded use, it occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:29; the reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation. Its central sense remains deprivation or bereavement.

Euilmarōdach, also rendered Eilmarothakh, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 25:27. Because the available information gives the name and its reference but not the verse text, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage rather than from the name itself.

This adjective means “fashionable,” describing someone or something regarded as stylish or in keeping with accepted fashion. It identifies an outwardly appealing or socially admired quality rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 11:25, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains being considered attractive, well-regarded, or suitably fashionable.

Ēram, also rendered Iram, is a proper name used for people named in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times in the LXX corpus, across 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, the particular person identified must be determined from each passage’s context.

This adjective describes something lethal—something capable of causing death. It is used as a describing word rather than as the name of a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Numbers, Job, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense remains the same: deadly or fatal in effect.

This adjective means “divine,” describing what belongs to, comes from, or is associated with God or the divine realm. It identifies a quality rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 27 times, including uses in Proverbs, Isaiah, and several Maccabean books. Its precise force depends on the noun or idea it describes, but its central sense remains a connection with the divine.

This verb means “warm”: to make something warm or to become warm. It describes a change involving heat, whether a person, an object, or something being heated. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 13 times, so its meaning is established across several passages rather than being limited to one unusual use. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being warmed and the surrounding sentence.

This word means a shield: a defensive piece of equipment used to protect a person in battle. It is a noun referring to the object itself, whether one shield or several shields. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times across 20 verses, showing that it is a normal word for battlefield protection and military equipment. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a shield used for defense.

Iachoum, also rendered Iakhum, is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Kings 7:7. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role in that verse cannot be described further here.

Idai is a proper name, identified also as Ithe. It functions as a name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:14, and is rendered “Idai” there. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise referent must be determined from that passage’s context.

Iermouth, also rendered Iermuth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:35. Its precise referent and significance must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, rather than from the name alone.

This verb means “sit down,” describing the act of taking a seated position. It is a straightforward action word rather than a title, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Proverbs, so its exact force in either passage comes from the surrounding sentence and scene. The word itself contributes the basic movement or action of settling into a seated position.

The word means “bend down.” It is a verb describing the physical act of lowering or leaning the body toward a lower position. In the Greek biblical corpus represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Psalms and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is concrete and action-focused. The surrounding verse determines the precise setting in which someone or something bends down, but the word itself points to a lowered posture or movement.

This Greek LXX noun means “destruction,” referring to ruin or the bringing of something to an end. It names an outcome rather than an action or quality, so it points to what is lost, overthrown, or brought to ruin. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Psalm 51:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains destruction or ruin.

This verb means “cross-breed with,” describing the act of breeding one kind of animal with another. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 19:19. The word’s basic sense is precise and limited: it identifies interbreeding with another kind, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific instruction or setting in which the action is mentioned.

This word means “of horn” or “made of horn.” It describes something connected with, formed from, or consisting of horn. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 22 times across 20 verses, with occurrences from Judges through Psalms. Its uses commonly relate to horn objects, and the word functions as a noun in the lexical record. The surrounding verse determines whether it refers to one horn, multiple horns, or an object associated with horn.

This noun means “ivy leaf,” referring to a leaf from the ivy plant. It names a physical botanical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:29. The word’s precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context, which are not included here. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: an ivy leaf.

This verb means “scrape,” describing the action of rubbing or removing something from a surface. It presents a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 7:14. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the action functions there, but the word’s basic meaning is the act of scraping.

This Greek LXX noun means “hiding place” or “lurking place”—a concealed location where someone or something remains out of sight. It refers to a place of concealment rather than to the act of hiding itself. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 1 Maccabees, and its basic meaning remains consistent across those occurrences. The surrounding verse determines who or what is concealed, but the word itself identifies the hidden location.

Lakei, also rendered Laki, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of name it is. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:19. Its precise referent and significance must therefore be determined from that passage’s surrounding text, which is not included here.

This word means “spear,” a weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or throwing. As a noun, it refers to the physical weapon itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 11 times, including passages mentioning soldiers, defenders, and instruments of attack. Its normal sense remains straightforward: a spear used in warfare or combat. The exact force of the word in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “reviling”: insulting, abusive speech directed against someone. It describes the act or expression of treating another person with contempt through harsh words. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across Exodus, Numbers, Proverbs, and Sirach, showing its use in several settings involving hostile or dishonoring speech. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means malady: a condition of sickness or illness. It refers to bodily affliction rather than naming a person, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times across 14 verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, 2 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its exact force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a sickness or troubled physical condition.

This verb means “learn”: to come to know or understand something through receiving instruction or gaining knowledge. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 54 times, so it describes a recurring act of acquiring understanding rather than a single specialized action. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being learned and the surrounding wording. The word is rendered “learn” in the available translation evidence.

This verb describes something joined or constructed by connecting it with beams. It presents the beams as the means that hold parts together, emphasizing a built or structural connection rather than a loose association. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 7:42, and its ordinary meaning is simply “connected by beams.” The surrounding verse would be needed to explain which structure or objects are being described there, but the word itself points to beam-supported construction.

This word means “only child,” describing someone who is a person’s sole child. As an adjective or noun, it identifies the child as unique within the family rather than one among several children. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Judges, Psalms, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a single, unmatched child. [p03:word:lxx:L708996:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L708996:occurrences]

This word means a fly, the small flying insect. It is a noun used for one insect or for flies in the plural, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from 2 Kings, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about the insect. The word’s gloss and short definition are both “fly.”

“Nachaligaias; Nakhaliyeas” is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, quality, or relationship, so its meaning is primarily the identification of the individual who bears the name. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 23:30. The available information does not provide the surrounding verse text, so the person’s specific role cannot be explained here.

This noun means “legislation”: lawmaking or an established body of laws. It names legislation as a subject or reality rather than describing an action by itself. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 and 4 Maccabees. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “drink wine.” It describes the act of consuming wine and functions as an action word rather than a name for a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 31:4. The word’s basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular instruction or significance attached to that action. Its exact force in Proverbs 31:4 must therefore be understood from the verse and its immediate context, not from the verb alone.

This word means “angrily.” As an adverb, it describes an action or speech done with anger, showing how someone acts rather than naming the person or feeling itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains clear: the action is carried out in an angry manner.

The word is a proper name, rendered “Oulai” or “Ule.” It functions as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 8:16. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific referent cannot be explained further here; its supported meaning is the named designation itself, preserved in these two renderings.

Ochchophpha, also rendered Okhkhoffa, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Chronicles 24:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise referent cannot be identified more specifically from this word alone.

gl: of mingled tribes; of all sorts
d: of mingled tribes; of all sorts

e.t: This word describes people or things drawn from mixed tribes, or more broadly, of all sorts. It can function as an adjective describing a group or as a noun referring to such a mixed group. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Deuterocanonical books. Its central idea is variety within a group rather than one single tribe, kind, or origin. The surrounding verse determines exactly what group or collection it describes.

This Greek LXX noun means a comforter: someone who brings consolation or encouragement to another person. It describes a person in the role of giving comfort, rather than an emotion or an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 16:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic meaning remains a person who offers comfort.

This verb means to “push aside” or “reject,” describing the act of refusing something or moving it out of the way. It expresses a deliberate response rather than merely passing by or overlooking something. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains setting something or someone aside instead of accepting or retaining it.

This Greek LXX verb means “scrape off”: to remove something by rubbing or scraping it from a surface. It describes an action rather than an object, so its basic sense is the physical act of stripping away an outer layer or attached material. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Wisdom 13:11. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself centers on removal by scraping.

This verb means “broaden”: to make something wider, more spacious, or more open. It describes an enlarging action rather than a fixed object, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being widened. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 22 times, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and later writings. Its basic sense remains the act of extending or opening out; the precise subject and purpose come from each passage’s context.

This noun means “flock,” referring to a group of animals kept or traveling together. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in Genesis 32:17. The word identifies the animals collectively rather than one individual animal. Its exact significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning remains a flock or herd-like group under consideration as one unit.

This adjective describes someone or something belonging to war or associated with warfare. It identifies a war-related quality rather than naming an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs 37 times, with most occurrences in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the person or thing being described, but its central sense remains firmly connected with war.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Sale
e.t: This noun means “sale”: the act or transaction of selling something. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it is used 21 times for the idea of something being sold or transferred in exchange, including property and goods. Its use in Genesis and Leviticus shows that it belongs to ordinary economic and legal language. The precise force in any verse depends on what is being sold and the surrounding passage.

This verb means “know beforehand”—to have knowledge of something before it happens or is encountered. It describes prior awareness rather than merely learning something at the moment. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:1. The word’s basic sense remains focused and specific: knowing in advance. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the lexical idea is clear.

This verb means “held by.” It describes a person or thing in a state of being held by someone or something else. The wording focuses on the one being held, not on the holder. It is a Greek LXX verb and occurs only once in that corpus, at 2 Maccabees 5:18. The surrounding verse is needed to identify what or who is held.

This noun means “fright”: a feeling of sudden fear or alarm. It names the experience of being frightened rather than describing an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 3:25. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic meaning remains fright or fearful alarm. It is therefore a straightforward word for an inward response of fear. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L711064:identity; p03:word:lxx:L711064:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L711064:reference:0]

The word means “resh,” a noun used as a name or designation. Its meaning is therefore concise and specific: it identifies resh rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:153. Because no verse text is included, the surrounding use cannot be explained further; the lexical sense remains the name “resh.”

This word is a proper name rendered “Saphek” or “Safek.” It identifies a specific named person, place, or group rather than expressing an action or quality, though the available lexical information does not specify which kind of entity it names. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:28. Its precise referent must be identified from that passage’s verse text and surrounding context.

Sidē, also rendered Sithi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament-related corpus, but the available information does not provide enough verse text to specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 15:23. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since a proper name receives its full identification from context.

This word means “you,” referring to the person or people being addressed. As a pronoun, it directs speech, instruction, questions, promises, or other words toward someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 1,277 times, showing that it is a common way to identify the one receiving spoken or written address. Its exact force—whether singular or directed to more than one person—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Spania is a proper name for a place. It identifies a geographic location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:3. The word itself supplies the place name, while the surrounding verse determines how that location functions in the passage. Because the verse text is not included here, its broader significance in that passage cannot be stated from the word alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread” or “make up,” describing the act of laying something out or arranging it. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, in Proverbs 15:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic sense remains the arranging or spreading of something into place.

This verb means “drink with”: it describes sharing a drink with another person or group. It presents drinking as an action done together, rather than merely drinking by oneself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Esther 7:1. The available wording identifies the shared action, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific occasion or significance of that drinking. This Greek LXX verb means “muster” or “numbered among”: it describes counting people as part of an organized group. In its three occurrences, all in Numbers, it concerns people being counted within Israel’s tribal or community totals. The word therefore focuses on inclusion in an official count or muster, rather than merely noticing or listing someone casually. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal sense is to count people as members of a recognized group.

Sōbēk, also rendered Sovik, is a proper name referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:25. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it does not establish the person’s role or significance there. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Sōbēk or Sovik.

This adjective means “quick,” describing someone or something that acts, moves, or happens without delay. It can point to speed or promptness, depending on the sentence around it, rather than naming a particular action by itself. In this LXX corpus, it occurs six times across Proverbs, Isaiah, Habakkuk, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any individual verse is determined by the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means to castigate or punish someone. It describes the act of imposing correction or penalty rather than merely experiencing hardship. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic sense is consistently connected with disciplinary treatment. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “bring.” It describes the action of bringing something or someone from one place or situation to another. As a verb, it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: twice in Deuteronomy 1:31 and once in 2 Maccabees 7:27. The surrounding verse text would determine the specific object or circumstances involved in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun describes “contempt” or “haughtiness,” expressing a proud, disdainful attitude that looks down on others. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 20:4. The word names more than simple disagreement: it points to proud disregard or scorn toward another. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains contemptuous haughtiness.

This noun refers to “pomp,” an impressive display, or an “apparition,” something that appears or is seen. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times, in passages from Habakkuk, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its central idea concerns an impressive appearance or visible manifestation, rather than an action. The surrounding verse determines whether it points more toward outward splendor or toward an apparition. Its uses are found in four Old Testament passages and one passage in Wisdom.

This noun means “brilliance”: shining brightness or radiant splendor. It describes the visible quality of something that gives off strong light, whether associated with the heavens, a storm, or another powerful display. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 23 times across 22 verses, showing that it can describe brilliance in more than one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This LXX noun appears to mean “excommunication,” though the available wording marks that meaning as uncertain. It names a form of exclusion or removal from the religious community rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs only once, in Jeremiah 44:16. Its exact force in that passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “useful; assist”: it describes helping, benefiting, or serving a useful purpose. It may refer to what provides practical help or to the act of assisting someone. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, appearing across books such as Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains usefulness or assistance.
